title: Generalized Mean-Field Ising Model as a Benchmark Family with Exact Solutions
authors: Madita Willsch, Gopal Chandra Santra, Dennis Willsch, Samuel Morales, Lukas Mauth, Vrinda Mehta, Fengping Jin, Kristel Michielsen
abstract: Exactly solvable models provide opportunities to understand complex optimization problems while offering controlled benchmarks for computational methods. However, nontrivial models that combine analytical tractability with challenging optimization structure remain scarce. Here, we introduce the Generalized Mean-Field Ising (GMFI) family, a densely connected and inhomogeneous class of Ising Hamiltonians whose ground states can nevertheless be obtained exactly. This exact solution reveals a hidden low-dimensional structure and enables a complete number-theoretic classification of different system sizes and degenerate ground states. Uniquely, the GMFI family can be used to benchmark both quantum and classical optimization methods over system sizes far beyond exact diagonalization. We investigate the GMFI family using several approaches, including theoretical analysis of quantum annealing, experiments on a D-Wave quantum processor, the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA), imaginary-time evolution (ITE), greedy algorithm, simulated annealing, and a quantum-inspired greedy algorithm. Despite the GMFI model's exact solvability, it exhibits nontrivial algorithmic behavior: although the quantum-annealing gap is expected to decrease with increasing system size, it shows pronounced and unexpected system-size-dependent oscillatory signatures. These results establish GMFI models as a rare bridge between exact many-body theory, number theory, optimization, and quantum hardware, providing a scalable benchmark for identifying and understanding algorithmic limitations in classical and quantum computing.
summary: This paper introduces the Generalized Mean-Field Ising (GMFI) model, an exactly solvable Hamiltonian used as a benchmark for quantum and classical optimization. By analyzing its ground state and its behavior under quantum annealing, the authors demonstrate that the model provides a powerful, scalable testbed for understanding algorithmic limitations in quantum computing.
main_problem: The paper aims to develop a benchmark family of models that combine analytical tractability with challenging optimization structure to test classical and quantum optimization algorithms.
main_result: The Generalized Mean-Field Ising (GMFI) model is shown to be exactly solvable, providing a scalable benchmark that exhibits unexpected system-size-dependent oscillatory signatures when tested with quantum annealing.
method: The authors combine theoretical analysis (number theory, algebraic methods) with computational approaches, including quantum annealing simulations on a D-Wave processor and classical optimization algorithms like QAOA and simulated annealing.
model_or_system: The system is the Generalized Mean-Field Ising (GMFI) model, described by a fully connected, inhomogeneous Ising Hamiltonian. This model is exactly solvable, revealing a hidden low-dimensional structure.
key_observables: Ground state energy, quantum annealing gap, magnetization ($M_0, M_1$), and the number of up spins ($K$).
important_parameters: System size ($N$), coupling constants ($h, J$), and the annealing time/schedule ($s$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the model can be mapped onto quantum hardware topologies (like Zephyr) and that the exact solvability provides a reliable benchmark despite algorithmic challenges.
figures_summary: Figure 1 shows the Hamiltonian structure for small N. Figure 13 displays the low-energy spectrum during quantum annealing, showing gap behavior vs. time for increasing N.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the exact solvability and ground state structure (Theorem 1) to deriving energy expressions in terms of macroscopic observables ($M_0, M_1$). It then investigates the model's behavior using various computational methods, culminating in detailed analysis of quantum annealing dynamics and number-theoretic classification of special cases.
why_interesting: The GMFI model serves as a perfect bridge, linking deep mathematical structures (number theory, exact solutions) to modern computational challenges (quantum annealing, optimization), making it highly relevant for testing quantum hardware capabilities.
